name: Northwest Face

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed pullout on SR-20 about 1 mi west of Washington Pass; Northwest Forest Pass required, privy at the lot.
waypoints.directions: The Blue Lake Trailhead is a signed pullout on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,400 ft. Make sure you are on the west side of the pass: the hairpin pond pullout east of Washington Pass is a different lot, used by the East Face routes. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here, and there is a privy at the lot.

waypoints.name: Stream crossing near meadow
waypoints.note: Small stream just before the climbers' path splits off the Blue Lake Trail — last reliable water before the dry talus approach.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail from the lot, climbing at an easy grade through forest for about 1.5 miles until it opens out into a small meadow under the Liberty Bell group. The stream sits right at that clearing. Fill here: the climbers' path above is dry all the way to the base.

waypoints.name: Climbers' path junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Blue Lake Trail here onto the signed climbers' path (Liberty Bell Trail #727) through slabs, talus, and meadow toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.
waypoints.directions: Carry on a minute or two past the stream and watch on the left for the climbers' path leaving the graded tread. A large wooden sign for Liberty Bell Trail #727 marks it, and it is well beaten once you are on it. If you are still walking smooth trail heading for Blue Lake, you have gone past it.

waypoints.name: Approach gully rockfall zone
waypoints.note: Gully below the notch holds snow into late June and sheds rock heavily once it melts out; stay on the boot path that breaks off before the loose gully proper.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path up through slabs, talus and heather benches, trending toward Concord Tower. It steepens as it enters the drainage below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Put helmets on before you commit to that ground — anything released here funnels straight down the gully onto whoever is below.

waypoints.name: Break-off below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
waypoints.note: Leave the climbers' trail here, a few hundred feet below the notch: scramble left over a short low-fifth-class step onto the sloping west-side bench to reach the NW aspect instead of continuing up the gully to the Beckey start.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the climbers' trail as it climbs toward Concord for as long as it reasonably holds, rather than dropping into the gully bed and following it up. The break onto the northwest side comes below the notch, not in it: a couple of hundred feet short of where the Beckey Route starts, where the gully visibly splits.

waypoints.name: West-side bench traverse
waypoints.note: Exposed leftward traverse across slabs and thin timber below the face to gain the start of the NW cracks/corners; loose blocks noted in route descriptions.
waypoints.directions: From the split, scramble up and left over one short step of easy fourth or low fifth class rock — about ten feet of it, and if you are climbing much more than that you have missed the spot. That gains the broad sloping bench on Liberty Bell's west side. Traverse left along the base of the slabs and up through thin timber and larch groves to the left-leaning crack and groove where the face begins.

waypoints.name: Liberty Bell summit
waypoints.note: True summit; descend the Beckey side: a short downclimb or rappel to a ledge, a single-rope rappel from a slung tree, then one double-rope or two single-rope rappels from bolts to the notch.
waypoints.directions: Five pitches: a left-trending gully and crack past a couple of trees, then a crack system left of the small chimney with a horn to pull over, then a left-facing corner of large thin flakes — stay right on the good flake rather than the middle splitter, which is much harder. The long north-facing dihedral above is the crux and can stretch a 60m rope. Easy ground up and left gains the west summit, and a short scramble from there reaches the true summit.

approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft, on WA-20 about 1 mi west of Washington Pass), follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.5 miles through forest to a small meadow/clearing below Liberty Bell. Leave the Blue Lake Trail here on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits left just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus, and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Rather than dropping into the main Beckey/Liberty Bell-Concord gully, the NW Face approach stays on the climbers' trail as it climbs toward Concord as long as it reasonably can, then breaks left onto a short, well-trodden low-5th-class step (no more than about 10 ft of easy 4th/low-5th climbing — if you're doing more than that you've missed the spot) that gains the little-visited NW plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of larch groves below the northwest face proper. Total gain to the base is on the order of 2,000+ ft over roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully section below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts out, so helmet up through the talus and gully approach; the Access Fund/Washington Conservation Corps have done trail work here to reduce loose-rock exposure.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path toward Concord, then the ten-foot step onto the northwest plateau
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles through forest to a small meadow below Liberty Bell. This is the opposite trailhead from the hairpin pond pullout used by the east face routes.

Leave the Blue Lake Trail on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits left just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Roughly 2,000-plus ft of gain over 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts, so helmet up through the talus and gully.
hazards: A rockfall-prone approach gully that holds snow into early summer
A ten-foot step that is easy to overshoot, leading parties onto harder ground
Queues at the popular Beckey rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep
One pitch of the descent can run slightly over 60 m, so a single-rope party may have to downclimb a short section
A loose gully downclimb from the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The entire find is a ten-foot step, and the route's own description makes it a negative test: if you are climbing more than about ten feet of easy fourth or low-fifth class to gain the plateau, you have missed the spot.

How you get to it: rather than dropping into the main Beckey and Liberty Bell-Concord gully, stay on the climbers' trail as it climbs toward Concord for as long as it reasonably can, then break left onto that short, well-trodden step. The step gains the little-visited northwest plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of larch groves below the northwest face proper.

So there are two confirmations and both work without seeing the summit: the step is ten feet and well-trodden, and above it you are standing on a bench with larch trees on it. Larches on a bench, on the northwest side, below a wall, is the plateau.

The negative test against the other routes off this path, which is where parties actually go wrong: if you have dropped into the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord and are climbing scree toward a notch, you are on the Beckey Route and Overexposure approach, not this one. This route never enters that gully.

Where the day ends up, which is not where it started: from the west summit you downclimb and scramble to the top of the Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the northwest face. Rappel about 20 ft down the upper Beckey pitch to a ledge, traverse left, east, to a tree hung with rap slings, one single-rope 60 m rappel to a flatter stance, then a double-rope rappel from a bolted anchor to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft, and downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers' path.
